exercises.title: Understand a consumer's day
exercises.job: Tell what you saw from what you were told, and find what is still missing.
exercises.scenario: You followed Priya, a 22-year-old final-year student in a hostel, for one day and interviewed her at the end. The notes below are made up for practice. Sort what you can say about her.

material.label: Observed
material.text: 8:10: skipped breakfast and bought tea at the canteen. 10:00: watched lecture recordings at 1.5× speed with earphones. 14:00–16:00: sat in the library with her phone face down. 23:40: ordered a snack from a delivery app and used a 40% coupon at checkout.

material.label: She said
material.text: "I never have time to cook." "I only order when there is a coupon." "Everyone in my hostel orders late at night."

claims.text: She ordered a snack at 23:40 using a 40% coupon.
claims.why: It was observed, with a time and a detail. It describes one evening.

claims.text: She kept her phone face down for two hours in the library.
claims.why: It was observed and has a time range. It does not say why she did it.

claims.text: She says she only orders when there is a coupon.
claims.why: It is what she said. It may not match what she does. Her order history would check it.

claims.text: She says she never has time to cook.
claims.why: A statement. It may be true, and it may be a convenient reason.

claims.text: She orders late because delivery apps are the only food available then.
claims.why: Nothing in the notes says what else was open or what the canteen hours are. It is a guess about her reason.

claims.text: Students like her are price-sensitive about everything.
claims.why: It generalises from one person and one coupon. It is an assumption about a large group.

claims.text: All hostel students order late at night.
claims.why: It is her claim about other people. Treat it as a lead and check with others.

claims.text: If we show a coupon to hostel students who have not ordered that day, at 22:00, more of them will order than a similar group with no coupon, measured over two weeks.
claims.why: It names a change, an expected result, a comparison group and a measure. It can fail.

evidenceNeeded.text: Her order history for a month, with and without coupons
evidenceNeeded.why: It shows whether she orders only with coupons, so it tests her statement against behaviour.

evidenceNeeded.text: What else is open near the hostel at 23:40, and the canteen hours
evidenceNeeded.why: It tests the assumption that delivery is her only option.

evidenceNeeded.text: Interviews with eight other hostel students
evidenceNeeded.why: It tests whether her story holds for others.

evidenceNeeded.text: Her age and year of study
evidenceNeeded.why: You already have it, and it does not change what to do next.

evidenceNeeded.text: The app's total downloads in her city
evidenceNeeded.why: It is a large number that says nothing about why she orders.

hypothesisOptions.why: It has no measure and cannot fail. It describes a taste, not a testable change.
It is a broad claim with no change, group or measure.

hypothesisOptions.text: If hostel students see a 40% coupon at 22:00 on days they have not ordered, more of them order that night than a similar group without it, over two weeks.
hypothesisOptions.why: It states the change, the group, the comparison and the measure.

takeaways: A fact has a source and a context. A statement is what someone said.
One person is a lead, not a pattern.
A good hypothesis names a change, a comparison and a measure.
Ask what evidence would change your mind before you decide.

exercises.title: Investigate a purchase decision
exercises.job: Work out why someone bought, using what they did and not only what they said.
exercises.scenario: A first-time buyer of running shoes spent three days choosing. The notes are made up for practice. Sort what you can say about why she bought online.

material.label: Observed
material.text: Day 1: read reviews on two sites for 40 minutes. Day 2: visited a store, tried on three pairs, bought nothing, took a photo of one pair. Day 3: ordered a different colour of the same model online at 12% less than the store price.

material.label: She said
material.text: "The store is too expensive." "I wanted to be sure about the fit first." "My friend said colours look different in photos."

claims.text: She tried on three pairs in a store and then bought online.
claims.why: It was observed. The order of events is clear.

claims.text: The online price was 12% lower than the store price.
claims.why: It is a measured price difference for the same model.

claims.text: She says the store is too expensive.
claims.why: It is her explanation. The 12% difference is a fact, but price may not be the whole reason.

claims.text: She says she wanted to be sure about the fit first.
claims.why: A statement. It matches her trying on shoes, which is a behaviour that supports it.

claims.text: She bought online because it was cheaper.
claims.why: The price gap is a fact, but the reason is not established. She also said she wanted the fit checked, and she changed the colour.

claims.text: Shoppers always try in a store and buy online.
claims.why: It generalises from one shopper to all. The notes do not support it.

claims.text: If the store offers to match the online price for shoppers who have tried a pair on, more try-ons end in a store purchase, measured over a month.
claims.why: It states a change, the group, the expected result and a measure.

claims.text: Two sites' reviews took 40 minutes to read.
claims.why: It was observed and timed.

evidenceNeeded.text: How many people who try on shoes in the store buy in the store, and how many buy elsewhere later
evidenceNeeded.why: It shows how common this path is, so you do not rely on one shopper.

evidenceNeeded.text: Whether shoppers who are offered a price match buy more often
Why she chose a different colour from the one she tried
evidenceNeeded.why: It checks whether fit was the only reason, and may reveal another need.
It does not help you understand the decision.

evidenceNeeded.text: The store's total sales last year
evidenceNeeded.why: It is a large number that does not explain this path.

hypothesisOptions.why: It is vague and has no change or measure.

hypothesisOptions.text: If we match the online price in store for shoppers who tried a pair on, more try-ons end in a store purchase, measured over a month.
hypothesisOptions.why: It names a change, a group and a measure, so it can fail.
It describes a person, not a test, and one purchase does not show a trait.

takeaways: A price gap is a fact. "She bought because of the price" is an assumption.
Behaviour and statements can support each other. Check that they do.
Describe the path, then ask how many people follow it.
Test a change before you build a policy around one shopper.

exercises.title: Learn from an extreme user
exercises.job: Use an extreme case to find a need that ordinary users have in a milder form.
exercises.scenario: Arun delivers food at night in the rain, on a bike with his phone on a mount. The notes below are made up for practice. Sort what you can say.

material.label: Observed
material.text: He wears thick gloves and taps with the knuckle. Three of ten taps on small buttons hit the wrong thing. He turns brightness to maximum and the battery shows 12% by midnight. In a basement car park the map stops loading and he waits about 30 seconds.

material.label: He said
material.text: "The app hangs in basements." "I use voice for the address when I can." "Other riders have the same problem."

claims.text: Three of ten taps on small buttons hit the wrong target while he wears gloves.
claims.why: It was observed and counted.

claims.text: The map stopped loading in a basement car park, and he waited about 30 seconds.
claims.why: It was observed with a place and a duration.

claims.text: He says the app hangs in basements.
claims.why: It matches what was observed, but it is his description.

claims.text: He says other riders have the same problem.
claims.why: It is a claim about other people. Check it with other riders.

claims.text: Riders do not like small buttons.
claims.why: It generalises from one rider in gloves. It may hold for riders in rain, and it may not.

claims.text: He uses voice because typing addresses is hard.
claims.why: He said he uses voice, but not why. The reason is a guess.

claims.text: If primary actions are larger and key screens work offline, riders complete a delivery with fewer mis-taps and less waiting, and other users do not complete fewer tasks, measured over two weeks.
claims.why: It names a change, two groups, and measures for both, including a check that ordinary users are not harmed.

claims.text: His battery showed 12% by midnight with brightness at maximum.
claims.why: It was observed. The cause of the drain was not established.

evidenceNeeded.text: Observe five more riders on shifts, in different weather
evidenceNeeded.why: It tests whether Arun is typical of riders or unusual.

evidenceNeeded.text: Mis-tap rates and task times for all users, split by screen size and by use of gloves if known
evidenceNeeded.why: It shows whether the need appears in milder form for ordinary users.

evidenceNeeded.text: How often the map fails to load, by location type

evidenceNeeded.why: It does not help explain the problem.

evidenceNeeded.text: How many riders the company employs in total
evidenceNeeded.why: It is a count, not evidence about the need.

hypothesisOptions.why: It is vague, with no change, group or measure.

hypothesisOptions.text: If primary actions are larger and key screens work offline, riders have fewer mis-taps and less waiting, and ordinary users complete the same number of tasks, measured over two weeks.
hypothesisOptions.why: It states the change, both groups, and measures, and includes a guard for ordinary users.
It describes one person and cannot guide a product change.

takeaways: An extreme user shows a need that others have in a milder form.
Check whether the extreme case generalises before you design for it.
Test that the change does not harm ordinary users.
